title: Jira vs Plane
comparison_markdown:
# Jira vs Plane (2026)

## Overview
Jira and Plane are two project management tools that help teams organize and track their work. This comparison is useful for teams considering switching from Jira to Plane, possibly due to the core use case of issue tracking and project management, and the key reason being the desire for more control over their data and costs. Teams who value self-hosting and customization may benefit from this comparison.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Jira has a per-user monthly fee, while Plane is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: Plane allows teams to have full control over their data, while Jira stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Jira has a more straightforward setup process, while Plane requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Jira is designed for large teams and enterprises, while Plane is more suitable for small to medium-sized teams.
* Integration with Git: Jira has native integration with Git, while Plane uses third-party integrations for Git support.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Jira | Plane |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.75-$14.50/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $387.50-$725/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,550-$2,900/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Jira:**
* Pros:
	+ Easy to use and set up
	+ Native integration with Git
	+ Scalable for large teams
	+ Wide range of third-party integrations
* Cons:
	+ Expensive for large teams
	+ Limited control over data
	+ Proprietary license
**Plane:**
* Pros:
	+ Free and self-hosted
	+ Full control over data
	+ Customizable and flexible
	+ Open-source license
* Cons:
	+ Requires technical expertise for self-hosting
	+ Limited native integrations
	+ May not be suitable for very large teams
	+ Limited support resources

## When to Choose Each
Jira is a good choice for large teams and enterprises that need a scalable and easy-to-use project management tool, and are willing to pay for the features and support they need. Plane is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams that value control over their data and customization, and are willing to invest time and resources into self-hosting and setup.
Plane is suitable for teams that require a high degree of flexibility and customization, and are comfortable with the technical requirements of self-hosting. Jira, on the other hand, is a better fit for teams that prioritize ease of use and scalability, and are willing to pay for the convenience and support that comes with it.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format.
2. Set up a Plane server and configure the necessary integrations.
3. Use the Plane import tool to import your Jira data.
4. Configure your Plane instance to match your Jira workflow.
5. Test and verify that all data and functionality have been migrated correctly.

## Our Take
Plane is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the features and polish of Jira. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Plane's self-hosting requirements can be steep, and may require significant technical expertise to set up and maintain. However, for teams that value control over their data and customization, Plane is a compelling alternative to Jira, and we recommend switching to Plane if you are a small to medium-sized team with simple project management needs and are willing to invest time and resources into self-hosting and setup.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) that don't need advanced features like native Git integration
* Teams that require full control over their data and are willing to self-host
* Teams with simple project management needs that don't require complex workflows
* Teams that are already familiar with self-hosting and have the necessary technical expertise
* Teams that are looking for a free and open-source alternative to Jira

## FAQ
### Can I migrate my Jira data to Plane?
Yes, you can export your Jira data in CSV or JSON format and import it into Plane using the Plane import tool.
### Is Plane suitable for large teams?
No, Plane is not yet suitable for very large teams, as it may not be able to handle the scale and complexity of their project management needs.
### Does Plane have native integration with Git?
No, Plane uses third-party integrations for Git support, rather than native integration like Jira.
### Can I self-host Plane on my own server?
Yes, Plane is designed to be self-hosted, and you can run it on your own server.
### Is Plane free?
Yes, Plane is free and open-source, with no per-user fees or licensing costs.

title: Trello vs WeKan
comparison_markdown:
# Trello vs WeKan

## Overview

Trello is a visual kanban board tool from Atlassian, simple and beginner-friendly. WeKan is an open-source kanban board offering the same card/list/board model without vendor dependency.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Trello paid plans start at $5/user/month; WeKan is completely free
- **Data control**: WeKan runs on your own server; Trello data lives on Atlassian infrastructure
- **Features**: Trello has a larger Power-Ups marketplace; WeKan covers core kanban features
- **Setup**: Trello requires zero setup; WeKan requires a server
- **Customization**: WeKan open-source code can be extended; Trello cannot

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Trello | WeKan |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $5+/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Trello

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### WeKan

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [wekan/wekan](https://github.com/wekan/wekan) * ~20k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Trello if:** Trello suits individuals and small teams wanting instant zero-setup kanban with integrations to Slack, Google Drive, and GitHub.

**Choose WeKan if:** WeKan is ideal for teams wanting full data ownership or air-gapped deployments.

## Migration Path

Export Trello boards as JSON, then use WeKan Trello importer in Settings to recreate boards, lists, and cards.

## Our Take

WeKan is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Trello tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your WeKan instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Trello, switching to self-hosted WeKan will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Trello until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Trello paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is WeKan free to use?
Yes. WeKan is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Trello to WeKan?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Trello data, follow the WeKan import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does WeKan get regular updates?
Yes. WeKan has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use WeKan without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if WeKan development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced June 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Trello](https://trello.com) and [WeKan](https://wekan.github.io) before making decisions.*

title: Dropbox vs Nextcloud
comparison_markdown:
# Dropbox vs Nextcloud (2026)

## Overview
Dropbox and Nextcloud are two popular cloud storage solutions that enable teams to store, share, and collaborate on files. This comparison is beneficial for individuals and organizations looking to switch from a proprietary cloud storage service to a self-hosted solution, with the core use case being secure and customizable file sharing. The key reason someone would switch is to regain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Dropbox charges a monthly fee per user, while Nextcloud is free to use with self-hosting.
* Data ownership: Nextcloud allows users to maintain full ownership and control over their data, whereas Dropbox's terms of service grant the company certain rights to user data.
* Setup complexity: Nextcloud requires more technical expertise to set up and configure, especially for self-hosting, compared to Dropbox's straightforward sign-up process.
* Scalability: Nextcloud can be more scalable than Dropbox, as users can add storage and resources as needed with self-hosting.
* Integration: Nextcloud has a built-in office suite called Nextcloud Office, whereas Dropbox relies on integrations with third-party services like Microsoft Office or Google Workspace.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Dropbox | Nextcloud |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $9.99-$16.58/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | AGPL 3.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | Approximately $499.50-$829/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | Approximately $1,998-$3,316/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Dropbox:**
* Easy to use and set up
* Wide range of integrations with third-party services
* Robust security features
* Real-time collaboration tools
* Limited control over data and customization options
**Nextcloud:**
* Self-hosting option for full data control
* High scalability and customization
* Integrated office suite and other apps
* Active community and regular updates
* Steeper learning curve and technical requirements

## When to Choose Each
When to choose Dropbox: Dropbox is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and don't require full control over their data. It's ideal for teams that already use a lot of third-party services and want to integrate them with their cloud storage. For example, a team of 10-20 users who only need basic file sharing and collaboration features may find Dropbox to be the better choice.
When to choose Nextcloud: Nextcloud is ideal for larger teams or organizations that require high scalability, customization, and control over their data. It's suitable for teams with technical expertise and resources to set up and maintain a self-hosted solution. For instance, a team of 50-100 users who need advanced security features and integration with their existing infrastructure may find Nextcloud to be the better choice.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Dropbox data in the ZIP format.
2. Set up a Nextcloud instance on your server or use a pre-configured appliance.
3. Use the Nextcloud WebDAV interface or the occ command-line tool to import your data.
4. Configure any necessary integrations and settings, such as user accounts and permissions.
5. Test your Nextcloud instance to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Nextcloud is a production-ready solution for most users, offering a wide range of features and a high degree of customization. However, it's essential to note that Nextcloud's self-hosting requirement can be a significant technical hurdle for some users. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Nextcloud's built-in office suite, Nextcloud Office, may not be as polished as some third-party alternatives.
Nextcloud is a viable option for users who value data control and customization, but it may not be the best choice for everyone. We recommend switching to Nextcloud if you're a technical user or have an organization with the resources to support self-hosting. However, if you prioritize ease of use and don't require full control over your data, Dropbox may still be the better choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Small businesses with 10-50 users who want to reduce costs and increase data control
* Large enterprises with 100+ users who require high scalability and customization
* Technical teams who need advanced security features and integration with their existing infrastructure
* Educational institutions with limited budgets who want to provide students with secure and customizable cloud storage
* Non-profit organizations with specific data control and compliance requirements

## FAQ
### Can I use Nextcloud with my existing Dropbox account?
No, you cannot directly use your existing Dropbox account with Nextcloud. However, you can export your Dropbox data and import it into Nextcloud.
### Is Nextcloud free to use?
Yes, Nextcloud is free to use, but you'll need to cover the costs of self-hosting, such as server maintenance and storage.
### Can I integrate Nextcloud with third-party services?
Yes, Nextcloud has a wide range of integrations with third-party services, including office suites, productivity tools, and more.
### Is Nextcloud suitable for small teams?
Yes, Nextcloud can be suitable for small teams, but it may require more technical expertise to set up and maintain compared to Dropbox.
### Can I use Nextcloud on mobile devices?
Yes, Nextcloud has mobile apps for Android and iOS, allowing you to access and manage your files on the go.
meta_description: Nextcloud, a free self-hosted cloud storage solution, offers more control and customization than Dropbox. See full comparison or Free migration guide.

### How hard is it to migrate from Zoom to Jitsi Meet?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Zoom data, follow the Jitsi Meet import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Jitsi Meet get regular updates?
Yes. Jitsi Meet has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.
